meta.title: Regex engines on every platform: ECMA-262 compliance and performance
meta.lede: How closely the regular expression engines of each platform follow ECMA-262, and how fast they are. Engines that implement ECMA-262 and each platform's other regex engines appear side by side, with V8 as the common reference, judged on the ECMA-262 test data and timed over the Industry workloads of dotnet/performance. Every engine ran on this runner tonight, in one job, so a figure compares across languages as well as within one.
facts: GitHub-hosted ubuntu26 20261101.186.1, AMD EPYC 9V74 80-Core Processor, 4 cores
corvus-dotnet/ecma262-regex-test-data at cff0860b7e, the same for every engine
meta.method:
What this page shows. The regular expression engines of each platform, side by side: engines that implement ECMA-262 (the regular expressions of JavaScript), the platform's other regex engines, which implement other dialects, and V8, the engine of Node.js and Chrome, as the common reference. Each engine is judged on the ECMA-262 test data, whose answers are V8's, and timed over the Industry workloads of dotnet/performance. An engine that does not implement ECMA-262 is there for its speed alone. How each engine is called is in the list of engines at the foot of the page.

A figure is the time to count every match a global search finds over the whole text of a workload, moving on one character after an empty match as JavaScript's matchAll does, in nanoseconds per count. An ECMA-262 engine is given the workload's flags with u, and V8 the flags with g and u. An engine of another dialect is given the pattern as it is with the workload's i, m and s flags.

How it is measured. Every harness keeps to one protocol. The workloads run one after another, each in 3 rounds of every engine in turn, the order of the engines turned each round. Each turn is a process of its own, which warms the engine, times 7 passes of as many counts as fit in 0.7 s, and reports the median pass. An engine's figure for a workload is the median of its rounds, and its spread is the fastest and the slowest round; a figure whose spread is over 5% is listed in the facts. Work a program would do once per text, such as checking that bytes are UTF-8, is done before the timing starts.

Where the figures come from. This repository's nightly workflow runs each source's published container image, at its newest release, one after another in one job on one runner. Each image runs its engines and V8 over the workloads, then the ECMA-262 test data for compliance. So the figures of every engine run here were measured on one machine in one night's run. Anyone can add an engine: see implementing a source.

Compliance beside an engine's name is its result on the ECMA-262 test data: its right answers over every answer the data asks of it, counted by the data's own rule (tools/answers.py), so that an answer its runner did not ask counts against it as a wrong one does. Each test is asked over UTF-16 and over UTF-8, under each of the three grammars (u, v and the legacy one without either). Records and tests where V8 departs from ECMA-262 are left out for every engine. An engine leaves out nothing else unless it is of one of four kinds, each shown as a badge of what it leaves out: no UTF-8 (or UTF-16), where the engine has no interface in that encoding; no u, v (or another grammar), where it has no such mode; Unicode and a version, where its tables are of another version than the data's, so it is judged by that version's answers; and from exec, where it has no global search, replace or split of its own and the runner writes them over its exec. Each runner limits an engine to 2 s a match (or an equivalent limit on its work), and an answer that reaches the limit is unanswered. An engine that cannot be stopped in a match runs in child processes, whose watchdog ends one at such an answer, and the next goes on from the answer after it; once three answers of a record have reached the limit, the rest of that record is unanswered. The tooltip has the counts, the runner and the calls it makes. Counts worked out at an earlier commit of the data (for an engine too slow to judge every night) are a share of what that commit asks, and say which commit. "Not ECMA-262" marks an engine that implements another dialect.

> 30 s in a cell: the engine did not produce a result within 30 s. Every harness stops a figure that has not finished in 30 s and does not run it again in the workload's later rounds, so such a cell has no figure, and the engine is not ranked on that workload.

✕ in a cell: the engine failed on that workload, and has no figure there. Its tooltip says why: the pattern did not compile, the engine stopped with an error, or its count of matches differs from V8's, which is a wrong answer whatever the engine's dialect. An ECMA-262 engine's wrong count is also one more wrong answer in the compliance beside its name, so it is never 100%.

V8 appears once, from the .NET run.
